name: Time-saving bias
statement: Time saved by going faster follows a reciprocal rule, and people judge it as though it were linear, so they underrate the gain when slow and overrate it when already fast.
meaning: The arithmetic here is not in dispute, which is what makes the bias unusually clean. Time saved over a fixed distance by raising speed from V1 to V2 is t = cD(1/V1 − 1/V2), where D is the distance and c converts the units. Journey time is the reciprocal of speed, so the same increment of speed buys less and less time as the starting speed rises. Adding 10 mph to 20 mph over 10 miles saves 10 minutes. Adding the same 10 mph to 50 mph over the same 10 miles saves 2 minutes. Peer and Gamliel report both figures. People behave as though the saving were roughly proportional to the size of the speed increase, so the initial speed drops out of the judgement. Svenson called the resulting description the Proportion heuristic and wrote it as t = cD(V2 − V1)/V2, which gives the time gained too little weight at low starting speeds and too much at high ones. Peer and Gamliel proposed a variant that divides by the initial speed rather than the higher one, and call it the Linear heuristic. Which of the two people use is unsettled, and Peer and Gamliel say so themselves. That they use something linear is the finding.

origin.note: The name is from this paper, and Peer and the Eriksson group both credit it with coining the term. The effect is older. Svenson's abstract points back to his own 1970 paper in the Journal of Experimental Psychology, which reported that estimated time savings follow the Proportion heuristic. The 1970 paper was not obtained on 21 September 2026, and the block met was a bot challenge at the publisher's front end rather than a paywall. Crossref, OpenAlex and PubMed hold no abstract for it, and the Internet Archive's microfilm copy of the issue is lending restricted. What it did is reported here from Svenson's 2008 abstract and from Eriksson, Svenson and Eriksson's 2013 description of it.

evidence: Svenson's 2008 abstract describes three studies. The first asked people to choose between road improvement plans and found that a Ratio rule, the choice form of the Proportion heuristic, predicted the wrong decisions. The second moved the problem to health care, asking which of two clinics to reorganise to free up more doctors' time. The third used a matching procedure in which participants equated two alternatives, and the results supported the Ratio rule. The body of the paper was not obtained, so the example that runs through the later literature is taken here from Peer. Peer reports that Svenson's participants preferred a plan raising mean speed from 70 to 110 kph to one raising it from 30 to 40 kph, and works the arithmetic over 10 km, where the first saves 3 minutes and the second about 5. Peer put the same claim through three studies in Judgment and Decision Making. Study 1, with 79 licensed drivers, found the bias whether people estimated time saved, distance coverable in a fixed time, or the speed needed to complete a distance in shrinking times. Study 2, with 139 drivers, found no major difference between a numeric response scale and a visual analogue one. Study 3 reclassified 159 drivers' answers from the first two studies against three models rather than two. More answers fitted a Differences pattern than the Proportion heuristic in all three questions, but the models overlapped on about 40% of them, and Peer declines to name a winner.

examples.tag: The last ten on the motorway
examples.text: A driver with thirty miles left lifts from 70 to 80 to make up time and gains about three minutes. From that starting speed the road is nearly out of minutes to give, and the expectation of arriving noticeably earlier comes from treating the gain as if it tracked the extra ten.

examples.tag: The slow end of the delivery round
examples.text: A driver averaging 15 mph through town over six miles dismisses lifting it to 20 as a waste of effort. It saves six minutes, more than the same increase buys anywhere on the fast roads. Gains are largest where the starting speed is lowest, which is where people expect least.

Moving a household from 5 to 20 megabits cuts a large download from about half an hour to seven minutes. Moving it from 100 to 200 is a far bigger step in the numbers on the bill and saves under a minute. The bill scales with speed and the waiting does not.

replication.headline: Found again by independent groups, in a national quota sample, in a driving simulator, and in taxis on the road.
replication.detail: Ray Fuller's group at Trinity College Dublin put four questions into a survey of 1,005 UK drivers, a representative quota sample, varying whether speed rose or fell and whether it started at 30 or 60 mph. Three of the four questions came out as predicted. A repeated-measures ANOVA showed no real appreciation of how starting speed bears on journey time, and a disordinal interaction showed drivers believing that a speed rise buys more time the faster one is already going, which is backwards. Gabriella Eriksson, Svenson and Lars Eriksson took 12 drivers into a fixed-base simulator at the Swedish National Road and Transport Research Institute, telling them neither the distance nor the time and leaving them only a speedometer. Each drove a distance at a set speed, then drove it again at whatever speed seemed necessary to gain exactly three minutes. From 30 kph they gained 6.14 minutes against a target of three (t(11) = 5.853, p = 0.0001, one-tailed). From 100 kph they gained 2.21 minutes (t(11) = -3.228, p = 0.0040, one-tailed). Asked afterwards, they put both drives near the three-minute target, judging 3.56 and 3.25 minutes. The same group later reported in Ergonomics that a control group with an ordinary speedometer repeated the pattern while a group shown inverted speed came closer to the target. Peer and Lidor Solomon boarded 30 Jerusalem taxis and interviewed the drivers mid-journey, comparing them with 30 non-professional drivers. Both groups overestimated the time an extra 10 or 20 kph would save, with an adjusted bias ratio of 2.41 for taxi drivers and 5.13 for car drivers, both above 1 (t(26) = 5.4 and t(28) = 4.69) and different from each other (t(54) = 2.86, p < .01). Peer and Eyal Gamliel ran the debiasing side across three samples, 91 and 68 American drivers on Mechanical Turk and 112 Israeli undergraduates, and found correct answers more common when a speedometer carried pace values as well as speeds. In the first sample, correct answers ran at 42.5% against 24.19% on the problem that raised speed from 20 mph, and at 28.02% against 13.75% on the problem that raised it from 50 mph.

study.cite: Fuller, R., Gormley, M., Stradling, S., Broughton, P., Kinnear, N., O'Dolan, C., & Hannigan, B. (2009). Impact of speed change on estimated journey time: Failure of drivers to appreciate relevance of initial speed. Accident Analysis & Prevention, 41(1), 10-14.

limits: The studies read here print almost no standardised effect sizes. The exceptions are the eta squared values Peer attaches to two comparisons that came out null, not to the bias itself, so no d or r is printed above and the structured fields are empty. Crossref, Europe PMC and the open web were searched on 21 September 2026 and hold no meta-analysis and no failed replication of the bias. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar refused their search endpoints that day with rate limits, so neither was re-checked. Authorship is concentrated: Svenson, Peer and the Eriksson group account for most of the record, and Fuller's survey is the one large test from an unrelated team. Its body was not obtained, and the abstract does not say which of the four questions failed. Peer's own Study 1 carried a question that ran the wrong way, in which drivers overestimated the time a cheetah saves over 100 metres from 50 kph. The simulator study had 12 participants, and one of its six men was replaced after driving flat out in both conditions; the authors report that keeping him would have strengthened the bias at 30 kph and weakened it at 100. Peer and Gamliel excluded 19%, 28% and 13% of their three samples for answers that violated the monotone relation between speed and time, and a further 33%, 19% and 7% did not finish every problem. The taxi study interviewed 30 drivers in one city, all men, against a student comparison group that was mostly women. Svenson's 1970 paper could not be obtained. Almost all the evidence is about driving. Svenson's clinic problem and a production-line problem described by Peer and Gamliel are the non-driving cases read here, and a 2020 paper in the International Journal of Project Management puts the bias in software projects, though it was not obtained either.
misreadings: The bias is not that people always overestimate time saved. It is directional, and the direction turns on the initial speed: underestimation from a low one, overestimation from a high one. Svenson's own 2008 abstract states the one-sided version, saying that people overestimate the time that can be saved, which is how the effect is usually passed on. A second error is reading the taxi field study as showing that drivers overestimate savings in general. Both groups there did overestimate, but the reason is visible in the same table. Taxi meters recorded a mean journey of 6.25 km in 12.7 minutes, an average speed of 29.6 kph, while all thirty taxi drivers overestimated their average speed, putting it at 68.83 kph on average. The starting speed they were reasoning from was more than double the real one, which puts them on the overestimating branch of a bias defined by starting speed. Nor does the bias say that speeding saves no worthwhile time. It says the opposite at the bottom of the range, where small increases save a great deal, and the road-safety interest is in the top of the range, where drivers expect a return that the arithmetic will not pay. The mechanism is also often stated with more confidence than the evidence carries. Svenson's Proportion heuristic and Peer and Gamliel's linear variant make different predictions, Peer's Study 3 could not separate them, and in Peer and Gamliel's own classification only about 67% of answers to one time-saving problem and about 40% to the other fitted any of their three models.
